summary: Sirach 27 warns that ordinary speech and trade expose a person’s character. The chapter moves from profit and hidden thoughts to foolish talk, betrayed friendship, deceitful plotting, and the way evil can return on the one who does it. It ends by naming wrath and anger as abominations possessed by a sinner.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom teaching at street level: buying, selling, conversation, friendship, secrecy, and resentment become tests of a wise life. It also continues the book’s concern that reverence for God must be visible in ordinary conduct.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the book was later translated into Greek by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, and everyday life taking place within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings, using comparisons from trade, nature, tools, speech, friendship, and social life.

outline.heading: Profit and the danger of sin
outline.note: The chapter opens by warning that the pursuit of wealth can bend a person away from righteousness, and that fear of the Lord is needed for stability.

outline.heading: Thoughts revealed by testing
outline.note: Sieve, furnace, fruit, and speech imagery show that a person’s inner life becomes visible when tested.

outline.heading: Righteousness, truth, and dangerous company
outline.note: The teacher contrasts those who follow righteousness and truth with fools, proud people, offensive talk, swearing, strife, and violence.

outline.heading: Secrets and broken friendship
outline.note: Revealing secrets destroys trust and can end a friendship as irreversibly as releasing a bird from the hand.

outline.heading: Deceitful speech and hidden traps
outline.note: The chapter describes a person who flatters in another’s presence but later twists speech and sets traps.

outline.heading: Evil returning on the evildoer
outline.note: Images of a falling stone, a pit, a snare, and waiting vengeance portray harm recoiling on those who plot or rejoice at another’s fall.

outline.heading: Wrath and anger
outline.note: The chapter closes by naming wrath and anger as abominations that belong to a sinner.

keyVerses.text: Unless a person holds on diligently to the fear of the Lord, his house will be overthrown quickly.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the opening warning by connecting moral stability with the fear of the Lord.

keyVerses.text: The fruit of a tree discloses its cultivation, so is the utterance of the thought of a person’s heart.
keyVerses.why: This saying gathers the chapter’s concern with speech: words reveal what has been growing inside.

keyVerses.text: He who reveals secrets destroys trust, and will not find a close friend.
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the chapter’s strongest section on friendship, secrecy, and the damage caused by betrayal.

keyVerses.text: He who digs a pit will fall into it. He who sets a snare will be caught in it.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter’s repeated warning that schemes of harm can turn back on the one who makes them.

themes: wrath and anger as destructive habits

questions.question: Why does the chapter start with profit and buying and selling?
questions.answer: The opening sayings treat commerce as a place where character is tested. The text does not say every exchange is sinful, but it warns that seeking to multiply wealth can make a person turn away, and that sin can press into the space between buying and selling.

questions.question: What does “fear of the Lord” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse it is the stabilizing allegiance that keeps a person from collapse. The chapter does not define the phrase at length, but it links it with diligence and with a house not being quickly overthrown.

questions.question: Why does Sirach use a sieve, a furnace, and fruit from a tree?
questions.answer: These comparisons all describe testing and disclosure. A sieve leaves refuse behind, a furnace tests vessels, and fruit reveals cultivation; in the same way, the chapter says thoughts and speech reveal the person.

questions.question: Does the chapter say people should be judged before they speak?
questions.answer: No. It says, “Praise no man before you hear his thoughts,” because speech is one way people are tested. The point is restraint in evaluation, not suspicion without evidence.

questions.question: Why are fools and proud people described through their talk?
questions.answer: The chapter presents speech as a public sign of wisdom or folly. Fools are associated with offensive talk, sinful laughter, swearing, and strife, while the proud are linked with conflict that can lead to bloodshed.

questions.question: Is revealing secrets treated as worse than ordinary conflict?
questions.answer: The chapter treats it as especially damaging because it destroys trust and close friendship. It says wounds and abuse may be followed by reconciliation, but the one who reveals secrets is “without hope,” meaning the friendship may not be recoverable.

questions.question: What kind of person is described as speaking sweetly and then twisting speech?
questions.answer: The chapter describes a deceptive person who flatters face to face and later turns another person’s words into a trap. It does not give a backstory for his motives; it focuses on the observable pattern of false friendliness and harmful speech.

questions.question: Does the chapter promise that every evil action visibly comes back at once?
questions.answer: The sayings use strong images of recoil: a stone falling on the thrower, a pit catching its digger, and a snare catching its maker. Readers differ on whether to read this as a general wisdom pattern or as a more direct claim about divine justice; the chapter itself stresses moral reversal without explaining timing.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with wrath and anger?
questions.answer: After many warnings about speech, betrayal, and revenge-like harm, the final verse names wrath and anger as abominations. It closes the chapter by turning from outward plots to the inner passions a sinner possesses.

glossary.def: Gain from trade or advantage. In this chapter it is a danger point because the pursuit of gain can lead people into sin.
Reverent allegiance to God that shapes conduct. In verse 3 it is connected with holding on diligently and with a household’s stability.
The inner reasoning or intention of a person. Verses 4-7 say thoughts are tested and disclosed, especially through speech.
Private matters entrusted to another person. The chapter says revealing them destroys trust and can ruin close friendship.
A trap. The chapter uses it for both escaped danger and the way a trap-setter may be caught by his own scheme.
